case_analysis.focal_point: Whether restitution imposed under the Mandatory Victims Restitution Act (MVRA) counts as criminal punishment such that retroactive application of MVRA restitution changes violates the Ex Post Facto Clause.
case_analysis.legal_provision: U.S. Const. art. I, § 9, cl. 3 (Ex Post Facto Clause) as applied to restitution imposed under the Mandatory Victims Restitution Act of 1996 (MVRA), Pub. L. No. 104-132, Tit. II, Subtit. A, 110 Stat. 1227 (codified primarily at 18 U.S.C. §§ 3663A, 3664).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Petitioner argues that MVRA restitution is a penal sanction imposed as part of the criminal sentence—mandatory, tied to conviction, administered and enforced through criminal-justice mechanisms, and historically understood as a form of punishment—so treating it as nonpunitive would improperly allow Congress to increase the consequences of past crimes retroactively without triggering Ex Post Facto scrutiny.
case_analysis.respondent_position: The United States’ litigating position evolved: in its brief in opposition it defended affirmance on the ground that even if MVRA restitution is punishment, the challenged retroactive change did not increase punishment in this case; after certiorari was granted, the Solicitor General notified the Court that the government would not defend the Eighth Circuit’s rationale and would instead support petitioner on the question presented, filing a merits brief supporting vacatur and taking the position that the Eighth Circuit’s nonpunitive characterization should not be maintained.
key_precedents: Smith v. Doe (intent-effects framework for determining whether a statutory consequence is punitive for Ex Post Facto purposes)
Kennedy v. Mendoza-Martinez (multi-factor test for punitive effect)
United States v. Bajakajian (constitutional treatment of monetary sanctions/punishment concepts relevant by analogy)
Paroline v. United States (modern Supreme Court discussion of criminal restitution’s function and limits)

John Roberts.reasoning: I remain with petitioner. The respondent’s best point—that restitution is compensatory and thus nonpunitive—cannot be reconciled with the MVRA’s operative design: it applies only upon conviction, is imposed “when sentencing,” is embedded in the criminal judgment, and is enforced through the criminal-justice supervision apparatus. As Justice Barrett emphasizes, those structural features are the statute’s legal effect, not mere labels, and treating them as nonpunitive would produce the improbable consequence of allowing retroactive increases in a mandatory component of a criminal sentence without Ex Post Facto scrutiny. Under the Smith v. Doe intent-effects framework, any remedial aim does not overcome the scheme’s conviction-triggered, sanction-like operation and traditional punitive objectives of deterrence and accountability.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Respondent’s best argument is that restitution is compensatory and therefore civil, but that relies on a label rather than the statute’s operative legal effect. As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Barrett explain, the MVRA mandates restitution “when sentencing a defendant convicted,” incorporates it into the criminal judgment, and enforces it through the criminal-justice apparatus—features that are quintessentially penal under our intent-effects inquiry. Permitting retroactive increases in this conviction-triggered, sentence-embedded obligation would invite an atextual evasion of the Ex Post Facto Clause, effectively allowing Congress to increase punishment for past conduct by recharacterization. The Constitution’s prohibition cannot be made to turn on such relabeling when the sanction is imposed as part of the sentence and backed by coercive penal enforcement.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: The respondent’s best contention—that restitution is merely compensatory and therefore not “punishment”—cannot be squared with the enacted text and structure Congress chose. As Justice Barrett stresses, the MVRA requires restitution “when sentencing a defendant convicted,” places it in the criminal judgment, and ties enforcement to the probation/supervised-release apparatus, which gives it unmistakably penal operation even if it also benefits victims. Chief Justice Roberts’s point is decisive that accepting a “civil” label here would create an easy loophole: Congress could retroactively increase a mandatory component of a criminal sentence simply by renaming it. Under the intent-effects framework, those conviction-triggered features and penal enforcement mechanisms are sufficient to treat an increased restitution obligation as increased punishment barred by the Ex Post Facto Clause.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: The respondent’s strongest point—that MVRA restitution is compensatory and therefore civil—cannot be squared with the governing intent-effects framework, which looks to how the sanction operates in law rather than the presence of a remedial aim. As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Barrett emphasize, Congress mandated restitution “when sentencing” upon conviction, embedded it in the criminal judgment, and made it enforceable through the supervision and penal machinery of the criminal system, all of which are classic indicia of punishment. Treating that scheme as nonpunitive would be not reasonably administrable because it would invite Congress to retroactively increase a mandatory component of a sentence by attaching a compensatory label, hollowing out the Ex Post Facto Clause. On these features, the MVRA change increases the legally prescribed consequences for past conduct and thus cannot be applied retroactively.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Respondent’s best argument—that restitution is compensatory and so categorically outside the Ex Post Facto Clause—falters under our intent-effects framework, which looks past labels to a measure’s design and operation. As the Chief explains, Congress made MVRA restitution mandatory "when sentencing" a convicted defendant, embedded it in the criminal judgment, and tied enforcement to the supervision and penal apparatus—features that are difficult to reconcile with a purely civil remedy. Justice Barrett’s point about the leverage of probation/supervised release (and the prospect of incarceration for willful noncompliance) underscores that the obligation functions as part of the punishment imposed for the offense, even if it also serves remedial ends. Accepting the compensatory label as dispositive would invite the very evasion the Clause guards against: retroactive increases in a core component of a criminal sentence by relabeling it nonpunitive.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The respondent’s strongest argument—that restitution is compensatory and thus nonpunitive—cannot carry the day once we attend to the statute’s text, structure, and operation. As Justice Barrett and the Chief emphasize, Congress made restitution mandatory “when sentencing a defendant convicted,” embedded it in the criminal judgment, and enforced it through the probation/supervised-release apparatus and other penal mechanisms—features that make it impossible to say the sanction is "solely" remedial. Under our intent-effects framework, labels and predominant purposes do not control when the consequence attaches only upon conviction and functions as part of the sentence. Allowing retroactive increases in such a conviction-triggered sentencing component would invite the very evasion the Ex Post Facto Clause exists to prevent, undermining the Constitution’s deep anti-retroactivity commitments.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: The respondent’s strongest point—that restitution is compensatory and therefore not “punishment”—cannot carry the day under our intent-effects framework. As the Chief Justice stresses, the MVRA makes restitution mandatory “when sentencing a defendant convicted,” embeds it in the criminal judgment, and enforces it through probation/supervised-release mechanisms with potential incarceration for willful noncompliance; those are classic penal administration features that defeat a purely civil characterization. Justice Barrett’s emphasis on the statute’s operative structure is especially persuasive because accepting a “nonpunitive” label here would create an administrable loophole allowing Congress to retroactively increase a core sentencing component by relabeling it. Given those effects and the finality-protecting function of ex post facto limits, retroactive application increasing restitution exposure is unconstitutional.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: The respondent’s strongest point—that restitution is compensatory and therefore civil—cannot overcome the MVRA’s text and placement: it is ordered “when sentencing a defendant convicted,” entered in the criminal judgment, and enforced through the supervision apparatus Congress chose. As Chief Justice Roberts stresses, those structural choices are not incidental; they define the legal consequence and make it implausible to treat restitution as a freestanding civil remedy for Ex Post Facto purposes. Justice Kagan’s emphasis on enforcement through probation/supervised release and the possibility of further penal consequences for willful noncompliance underscores the punitive effects that follow from conviction. Under our intent-effects framework, allowing retroactive increases to this mandatory, conviction-triggered component would invite the very evasion Justice Gorsuch identifies and hollow out the Clause’s protection against increased punishment for past conduct.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: The respondent’s best contention—that restitution is merely compensatory and thus nonpunitive—cannot carry the day in light of the MVRA’s operative text and legal effect. As Justice Barrett and the Chief Justice stress, Congress directed that restitution be ordered “when sentencing a defendant convicted,” incorporated it into the criminal judgment, and yoked it to coercive criminal-justice enforcement; those structural choices are strong evidence, under Smith v. Doe’s intent-effects framework, that the sanction functions as part of the punishment, even if it also serves remedial ends. Accepting a “compensatory” label as dispositive would, as Chief Justice Roberts notes, create an implausible loophole: Congress could retroactively increase a core sentencing component simply by renaming it, contrary to the Ex Post Facto Clause’s anti-retroactivity baseline. Reading the statute against that constitutional and common-law background, I remain persuaded that retroactive application of the MVRA’s mandatory restitution increase is barred.

John Roberts.reasoning: Applying the Smith v. Doe intent-effects framework, Congress designed MVRA restitution as a sentencing consequence triggered by conviction, administered through the criminal judgment, and enforced with criminal-law tools—features that reflect a penal choice rather than a freestanding civil compensation scheme. Functionally, the MVRA does not operate like a purely remedial measure “restor[ing] the status quo,” because it is mandatory, keyed to the offense of conviction, and imposed without the kind of victim-initiated process and individualized compensation features that typically mark civil remedies. Reading the MVRA in its statutory context—alongside fines and other sentencing provisions—treating restitution as nonpunitive would produce the improbable consequence that Congress could retroactively increase a core component of the criminal sentence while evading Ex Post Facto scrutiny, a result inconsistent with restraint in expanding prosecutorial and legislative leverage without clear constitutional limits. Because MVRA restitution is best characterized as criminal punishment, retroactive application that increases the restitution consequence for past conduct implicates the Ex Post Facto Clause.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The Ex Post Facto Clause is triggered only if the challenged consequence is “punishment,” and under the textually anchored Smith v. Doe framework the inquiry begins with Congress’s intent. Here, the MVRA restitution order is imposed as part of the criminal judgment at sentencing, keyed to conviction, and enforced through criminal-justice mechanisms—including the prospect of additional criminal sanctions for willful noncompliance—features that reflect a legislative choice to attach a penal consequence rather than a freestanding civil regulatory measure. Treating such restitution as nonpunitive would rest on an atextual, functional relabeling that underestimates the direct legal operation of the sanction and would allow Congress to increase the penal consequences of completed crimes without Ex Post Facto scrutiny. Because retroactive application would increase a component of the sentence, I would hold it is punishment and vote for petitioner.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: The Ex Post Facto Clause bars retroactive increases in criminal punishment, and restitution imposed under the MVRA is ordered as part of the criminal sentence, triggered solely by conviction, and enforced through criminal-justice mechanisms rather than ordinary civil collection. Applying the Smith v. Doe / Mendoza-Martinez intent-effects framework, whatever compensatory features restitution may have, its mandatory, conviction-based, and sanction-like operation makes it at least sufficiently punitive in effect that Congress may not apply expanded MVRA restitution obligations to pre-enactment conduct absent a clear constitutional basis. This is especially true where, on these facts, the change operates to increase the defendant’s legally enforceable financial liability compared to what could have been imposed when the offense was committed. Our precedents recognizing restitution’s punitive purposes confirm that the Eighth Circuit’s nonpunitive characterization cannot be sustained.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Applying the Smith v. Doe / Mendoza-Martinez intent-effects framework, MVRA restitution—imposed automatically upon conviction, incorporated into the criminal judgment as part of sentencing, and enforced through criminal-justice mechanisms—operates in form and effect like a penal sanction even if it also serves compensatory ends. That characterization is consistent with this Court’s repeated treatment of restitution as a component of the criminal sentence, including Paroline’s recognition that restitution is a penal, conviction-triggered consequence governed by criminal-law limits rather than a freestanding civil remedy. Because the MVRA’s mandatory scheme retroactively increases the consequences attached to the offense by altering the defendant’s sentencing exposure in a manner disadvantageous to the offender, applying it to pre-enactment conduct triggers and violates the Ex Post Facto Clause. The contrary “civil remedy” characterization is not doctrinally coherent with analogous sentencing precedents and would invite administrability problems by turning ex post facto scrutiny on indeterminate, case-by-case assessments of victim-compensation labels rather than the statute’s operative sentencing effects.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Applying the Court’s intent-effects framework (Smith v. Doe, guided by Mendoza-Martinez), restitution under the MVRA functions as criminal punishment: it is imposed only upon conviction, ordered by the sentencing court under criminal procedures, enforced through the criminal-justice system, and serves acknowledged penological ends like offender accountability and rehabilitation. That structure and function align with longstanding understanding—reflected in decisions like Kelly and reinforced in Paroline—that criminal restitution is part of the defendant’s sentence rather than a freestanding civil remedy. Given that punitive character, a retroactive MVRA change that increases a defendant’s restitution exposure for pre-enactment conduct triggers the Ex Post Facto Clause’s core prohibition on increasing punishment after the fact. Tradition and the centrality of sentencing limits to fair criminal adjudication counsel against allowing Congress to relabel a mandatory sentencing consequence as “nonpunitive” to evade ex post facto scrutiny.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The Ex Post Facto Clause codifies a core structural commitment against retroactively increasing the consequences that attend a criminal conviction, and here the MVRA restitution order is imposed only upon conviction, at sentencing, through criminal procedures, and enforced by the government using penal mechanisms—features that make it functionally part of the criminal sanction. Labels and even predominantly compensatory aims cannot control; the question is whether the scheme can “fairly be said solely to serve a remedial purpose,” and mandatory restitution pegged to offense conduct and imposed as a component of the sentence “serves in part to punish.” Applying the MVRA’s restitution changes to pre-enactment conduct thus operates retroactively in a way the Constitution disfavors and the Ex Post Facto Clause forbids when it increases the burdens attached to past crimes. The historically anchored understanding of restitution as a sentencing consequence, reflected in precedent treating criminal restitution as a “criminal sanction,” reinforces that this is not a novel expansion but a traditional application of the Clause to punishment following conviction.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: The Ex Post Facto question turns on whether the MVRA’s restitution is “punishment,” and under Smith v. Doe and Mendoza-Martinez the inquiry begins with legislative intent and then (if necessary) punitive effects. Here, the MVRA ties restitution to a criminal conviction and imposes it at sentencing through criminal-justice procedures, with enforcement mechanisms that operate through the criminal system—strong indicators that Congress made restitution part of the criminal penalty rather than a freestanding civil remedy. Even assuming some compensatory aim, the statute’s mandatory character and integration into the criminal judgment make it functionally punitive for Ex Post Facto purposes, so applying MVRA restitution changes retroactively would impermissibly increase the legal consequences of completed conduct. That conclusion follows from applying the Court’s established intent-effects framework and avoids creating an administratively unworkable carveout that would let Congress retroactively enhance sentencing consequences by relabeling them “restitution.”

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Start with the governing text and structure: the MVRA makes restitution mandatory “when sentencing a defendant convicted” of covered offenses and directs entry and enforcement of the order through the criminal judgment and supervised-release/probation apparatus—choices that Congress included, not incidental features we may disregard. That design links restitution to conviction and authorizes coercive, forward-looking criminal-justice tools (including revocation and incarceration for willful nonpayment), which signals punitive intent and effect under the whole statutory scheme rather than treating restitution as a freestanding civil remedy. Applying Smith v. Doe’s intent-effects framework, the Mendoza-Martinez factors confirm that MVRA restitution operates as punishment: it is imposed only upon a criminal conviction, advances traditional aims of punishment (deterrence and accountability), and is enforced through criminal supervision and restraints. Because it is punishment, a retroactive change that increases or newly mandates MVRA restitution for pre-enactment conduct triggers Ex Post Facto scrutiny, and the judgment characterizing MVRA restitution as nonpunitive cannot stand.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Starting with the MVRA’s operative text and placement in the sentencing scheme, Congress directed courts to order restitution “in imposing a sentence” on a convicted defendant, 18 U.S.C. § 3556, and made it mandatory for covered offenses, which situates restitution as a component of the criminal penalty rather than a freestanding civil remedy. Reading that text against the Ex Post Facto Clause’s background presumption that the government may not retroactively increase the punitive consequences attached to completed conduct, the relevant question is whether MVRA restitution is punishment under the intent-effects framework. The statute’s structure and enforcement mechanisms—imposition only upon conviction, administration through criminal sentencing procedures, and operation as a mandatory condition of probation/supervised release—give it at least significant penal effect even if it also serves compensatory aims. Because the MVRA change is being applied to pre-enactment conduct and increases the defendant’s mandatory sentencing consequences, it triggers Ex Post Facto scrutiny and cannot be sustained on a “nonpunitive” characterization.

case_analysis.focal_point: Whether restitution imposed under the Mandatory Victims Restitution Act (MVRA) is a criminal punishment such that retroactive application triggers the Ex Post Facto Clause.
case_analysis.legal_provision: U.S. Const. art. I, § 9, cl. 3 (Ex Post Facto Clause) as applied to restitution ordered under the Mandatory Victims Restitution Act of 1996 (MVRA), Pub. L. No. 104-132, Tit. II, Subtit. A, 110 Stat. 1227 (codified primarily at 18 U.S.C. §§ 3663A, 3664).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Ellingburg argues that MVRA restitution is penal in nature: it is imposed only after a criminal conviction, is mandatory and administered through criminal sentencing procedures, is enforced with uniquely penal collection mechanisms, and serves traditional punishment goals (deterrence, retribution, and rehabilitation) alongside victim compensation. Because it is punishment, applying MVRA restitution rules retroactively constitutes an ex post facto problem when the later-enacted rules increase the defendant’s financial exposure or lengthen/strengthen enforcement compared to the law in effect at the time of the offense.
case_analysis.respondent_position: The United States’ litigating posture evolved: in its brief in opposition, the government emphasized that the Eighth Circuit’s judgment should be affirmed because (even assuming restitution is punishment) the challenged retroactive application did not increase punishment in a way that violates the Ex Post Facto Clause. After certiorari was granted, the Solicitor General notified the Court that the government will not defend the Eighth Circuit’s rationale and will support petitioner on the limited question presented—i.e., that MVRA restitution should be treated as criminal punishment for ex post facto purposes—seeking vacatur of the lower-court reasoning.
key_precedents: Smith v. Doe (framework for distinguishing punitive vs. civil consequences; often used in ex post facto analysis)
Hudson v. United States (factors for determining whether a sanction is punitive or civil)
Kennedy v. Mendoza-Martinez (multi-factor test used to assess punitive effect)
United States v. Bajakajian (characterization of monetary sanctions as punishment in the constitutional context, particularly the Excessive Fines Clause)
Paroline v. United States (modern Supreme Court discussion of criminal restitution’s purposes/operation)
Pasquantino v. United States (restitution characterized as part of the criminal sentencing process in certain respects)
Kelly v. Robinson (criminal restitution’s penal character discussed in the bankruptcy-discharge context)

John Roberts.reasoning: The respondent’s strongest point is that restitution is compensatory and thus civil, but that label cannot overcome the MVRA’s text and operation: it is triggered only by conviction, imposed at sentencing, embedded in the criminal judgment, and enforced with criminal tools—features that, under our intent-effects framework, strongly indicate punishment for Ex Post Facto purposes. Justice Kagan’s emphasis on the statute’s sentencing-integrated administration is particularly persuasive in showing why this is not a freestanding civil remedy. At the same time, to preserve institutional legitimacy and avoid unnecessary constitutional pronouncements, we can adopt the narrow approach Justice Barrett and others endorse: hold only that retroactive application of MVRA provisions that increase a defendant’s sentencing consequences constitutes an ex post facto problem, without deciding restitution’s character across other constitutional contexts.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The respondent’s strongest contention—that restitution is “compensatory” and therefore civil—rests on a label that cannot override constitutional classification when Congress has made the obligation a mandatory consequence imposed “when sentencing a defendant convicted,” entered in the criminal judgment, and enforced through penal machinery. As the Chief Justice (Roberts) and Justice Barrett emphasize, the MVRA’s text and structure embed restitution in the criminal sentence, and we should not indulge an atextual recharacterization that would allow legislatures to aggravate criminal consequences retroactively by calling them “remedial.” The Ex Post Facto Clause draws a categorical line against retroactively increasing punishment; honoring that line also serves administrability and finality by preventing ad hoc, effects-balancing exceptions. A narrow holding—limited to the MVRA’s retroactive increase in sentencing consequences—adequately resolves the case without pronouncing on restitution in every context, as Justice Kagan notes.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: The respondent’s best point—that restitution is compensatory and thus “civil”—cannot overcome the MVRA’s enacted text and structure, which make restitution a mandatory consequence imposed “when sentencing a defendant convicted” and incorporated into the criminal judgment. As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Barrett emphasize, Congress embedded restitution in the sentencing machinery and tied enforcement to penal tools, and that contextual choice is hard to reconcile with the claim that the obligation is merely a freestanding civil remedy. Against the settled presumption against retroactivity (reinforced by the Saving Statute), I see no clear textual statement—no “plain import” or even “fair implication”—that Congress meant later MVRA provisions to aggravate consequences for pre-enactment conduct. Whatever compensatory aspect restitution may have, the statute’s operation as part of the criminal sentence is sufficient to trigger ex post facto scrutiny when retroactively applied to increase a defendant’s exposure.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: The strongest respondent argument is that restitution is primarily compensatory and therefore not “punishment,” but that characterization cannot survive the statute’s function and effects: the MVRA makes restitution mandatory upon conviction, embeds it in the sentencing judgment, and backs it with coercive penal mechanisms that can implicate liberty interests. Under our intent-effects framework (Hudson/Mendoza-Martinez), dual remedial and punitive aims do not erase punishment when the sanction is administered as part of the criminal sentence and carries classic penological purposes—deterrence and retribution—which our cases have recognized in this context. As Justice Kagan notes, the mandatory, sentence-integrated design and criminal enforcement tools are powerful indicia of punitive effect, and treating MVRA restitution as categorically “civil” would create an administrability problem by elevating labels over statutory structure and real-world consequences. Because retroactive application here increases the defendant’s punitive exposure relative to the law at the time of the offense, the Ex Post Facto Clause is implicated.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: The respondent’s strongest point—that restitution is compensatory and therefore civil—cannot be the end of the analysis under Hudson/Smith; we have to look to the statute’s design and real-world operation. Here, the MVRA is triggered only by conviction, imposed by the sentencing court as part of the criminal judgment, and enforced through distinctly penal mechanisms, which makes it hard to treat the increased exposure as anything other than an increase in punishment for Ex Post Facto purposes. Chief Justice Roberts’s proposed narrow framing is the right way to keep doctrinal coherence and administrability: we need decide only that retroactively applying a mandatory, sentence-integrated restitution regime that increases consequences for pre-enactment conduct implicates the Clause, without pronouncing on restitution’s character in every constitutional setting. Accepting a label-driven “compensation” carveout would invite evasion and inconsistency—precisely the kind of doctrinal instability our retroactivity and ex post facto cases have tried to avoid.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The respondent’s best point remains that restitution is “compensatory,” but labels cannot do the work the Ex Post Facto Clause forbids; we must look to how the law operates. As the Chief and Justice Barrett emphasize, the MVRA triggers only upon conviction, is imposed in the sentencing judgment, and is enforced with penal machinery—features that make it at least partly punitive, and that is enough for ex post facto scrutiny. Landgraf’s presumption against retroactivity reinforces the same conclusion absent a clear statement authorizing backward-looking increases in sentencing consequences. I also agree with Justice Kagan that adopting a label-driven exception would invite an unadministrable regime where legislatures can evade anti-retroactivity limits by calling punishment “compensation.”

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: The respondent’s strongest point is that restitution is compensatory and therefore civil, but under our intent-effects cases (Hudson/Smith) labels do not control when the sanction is triggered only by conviction, imposed in the sentencing judgment, and enforced through criminal mechanisms—features that strongly indicate punishment for Ex Post Facto purposes. Chief Justice Roberts’s proposed narrow framing is the right way to resolve the case: we need only hold that retroactively applying the MVRA regime to increase a defendant’s exposure compared to the law at the time of the offense implicates the Clause, without deciding restitution’s status across all contexts. That approach is administrable and prevents an evasion problem whereby Congress could aggravate sentencing consequences after the fact simply by styling them “compensatory.” Finality concerns cannot override the Constitution’s categorical bar on retroactively increasing punishment; they instead counsel for a tight, rule-based holding rather than an open-ended balancing test.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: The respondent’s strongest point—that restitution is compensatory and thus “civil”—cannot overcome Congress’s textual and structural choice to make MVRA restitution a mandatory consequence imposed “when sentencing a defendant convicted” and entered in the criminal judgment under § 3664. As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan emphasize, that sentencing-embedded design and penal enforcement machinery are powerful indicia of punishment under our intent-effects framework, at least for Ex Post Facto purposes. Accepting a compensatory label as dispositive would invite an unadministrable, exception-swallowing rule: legislatures could retroactively aggravate sentence-integrated obligations so long as they are styled as victim compensation. A narrow holding is appropriate: we need not classify restitution for all contexts, only that retroactively increasing this sentencing consequence constitutes an increase in punishment barred by the Clause.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: The respondent’s strongest contention—that restitution is essentially compensatory and therefore not “punishment” for Ex Post Facto purposes—cannot overcome the MVRA’s enacted design: it applies “when sentencing a defendant convicted,” is imposed through the criminal-judgment machinery, and is enforced with the sovereign’s penal tools. As Justice Kagan emphasized, that conviction-triggered, sentencing-embedded structure is a powerful indicator that Congress situated restitution within the criminal sanction, even if it also serves remedial ends. And Chief Justice Roberts’s narrow framing is the right one: we need decide only that retroactive application of an MVRA regime that increases a defendant’s sentencing exposure compared to the law at the time of the offense implicates the Ex Post Facto Clause. That conclusion follows from the statute’s text and the settled background principle that criminal-sentence components, imposed at sentencing and enforced as such, carry punitive character sufficient for ex post facto analysis.

John Roberts.reasoning: Under our ex post facto framework, the threshold question is whether Congress imposed a criminal punishment; if legislative intent is punitive, that largely ends the inquiry, and the MVRA by its terms operates as part of the criminal sentencing process and is triggered only upon conviction. Even if labeled compensatory, the statute’s mandatory character, its administration by sentencing courts, and its enforcement mechanisms tied to the criminal judgment reinforce that it functions as a penal sanction under the Hudson/Smith line, at least for ex post facto purposes. A narrow ruling is available: we need not decide every constitutional characterization of restitution, only that retroactive application of the MVRA’s restitution regime implicates the Ex Post Facto Clause when it increases the defendant’s punitive exposure relative to the law at the time of the offense. That approach aligns with precedent and protects institutional legitimacy by resolving only the question presented without upsetting broader restitution practice.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The Ex Post Facto Clause bars laws that retroactively increase “punishment,” and the proper inquiry is whether MVRA restitution, as imposed here through the criminal judgment, is part of the defendant’s criminal sentence rather than a freestanding civil remedy. Whatever compensatory effects restitution may have, Congress made it mandatory upon conviction and enforced it with the sovereign’s penal tools (including supervision conditions and criminal-judgment collection mechanisms), which places it within the traditional categories of criminal punishment, not merely a civil obligation. Under a historically grounded understanding of punishment and respecting separation of powers, courts may not recast this legislatively prescribed sentencing consequence as “civil” to avoid the Clause’s command when later-enacted MVRA rules increase a defendant’s exposure compared to the law at the time of the offense. Because applying the MVRA retroactively would attach a more burdensome punishment to completed conduct, it triggers the Ex Post Facto Clause.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: MVRA restitution is imposed only upon a criminal conviction, as part of the sentencing judgment, and is enforced through distinctly penal mechanisms (including supervision-related collection and contempt-like consequences), which strongly indicates that Congress treated it as a component of the criminal sanction rather than a freestanding civil remedy. Under the Ex Post Facto Clause—reinforced by the traditional presumption against retroactivity—Congress may not increase the punitive consequences attached to past conduct unless it has clearly made a nonpunitive civil scheme, and the MVRA’s text and operation point the other way. This Court’s cases have repeatedly recognized that criminal restitution, though compensatory in part, also serves classic penological ends (accountability, deterrence, retribution), and that dual purpose does not remove it from the category of punishment when it is administered as part of the criminal sentence. Accordingly, applying later-enacted MVRA restitution rules to pre-enactment offenses triggers ex post facto scrutiny because it retroactively alters the legal consequences of the offense by increasing punishment.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: The Ex Post Facto Clause’s threshold question is whether the challenged consequence is “punishment,” and MVRA restitution—imposed only upon conviction, integrated into the criminal sentencing judgment, and enforced through penal mechanisms that can jeopardize liberty (including revocation of supervised release for willful nonpayment)—operates as criminal punishment in purpose and effect. Even if Congress also sought victim compensation, this Court has repeatedly recognized restitution’s penological aims (deterrence and retribution) and its administration as part of the criminal process, which weighs heavily under the Mendoza-Martinez/Hudson functional inquiry. Because treating MVRA restitution as nonpunitive would require a hard-to-administer, label-driven carveout untethered from the statute’s structure and real-world consequences, I would classify it as punishment for ex post facto purposes. On that classification, retroactive application of later-enacted MVRA restitution rules that increase a defendant’s financial exposure or strengthen enforcement triggers ex post facto scrutiny.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: The Ex Post Facto Clause applies only to criminal punishment, so the threshold question is whether MVRA restitution is punitive under the Court’s intent-effects framework (Smith v. Doe; Hudson; Mendoza-Martinez) as administered in the criminal sentencing process. Whatever compensatory aims restitution may have, the MVRA makes it mandatory upon conviction, imposes it through the sentencing judgment, and enforces it with criminal-law mechanisms—features that, in both design and effect, align it with punishment rather than a freestanding civil remedy. That conclusion fits our own characterizations of federal restitution as serving penal purposes and as part of the criminal sentence, making retroactive increases in its scope or enforcement the kind of after-the-fact aggravation the Ex Post Facto Clause forbids. Given the Court’s repeated recognition that restitution “mete[s] out appropriate criminal punishment,” I would treat MVRA restitution as punishment for ex post facto purposes.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Under Landgraf’s deeply rooted presumption of prospectivity and our Constitution’s anti-retroactivity structure, the government may not apply later-enacted sentencing consequences to earlier conduct absent a clear statement—and here the question turns on whether MVRA restitution is punishment for Ex Post Facto purposes. Functionally, MVRA restitution is imposed only upon criminal conviction, as part of the sentencing judgment, in an adversarial proceeding prosecuted by the government, and enforced through uniquely penal collection and supervision mechanisms; whatever compensatory aims it may serve, it cannot fairly be said to serve solely a remedial purpose. Because the scheme serves in part to punish, retroactive application that increases a defendant’s exposure or enforcement burdens triggers the Ex Post Facto Clause’s categorical bar, and I would reject the lower court’s label-driven reasoning that treats MVRA restitution as merely civil or “make-whole.” A rule-like approach focusing on the statute’s real-world operation (rather than open-ended balancing over legislative motives) yields the administrable conclusion that MVRA restitution is criminal punishment in this setting.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: The Ex Post Facto Clause turns on whether the challenged measure is criminal punishment and whether the retroactive change increases that punishment; here, MVRA restitution is imposed only upon conviction, as a mandatory component of the criminal sentence, and is enforced through uniquely penal mechanisms—features that align restitution with punishment rather than a merely civil, compensatory remedy. Under the Smith v. Doe framework and the Mendoza-Martinez/Hudson factors, the statute’s operation and effects—mandatory imposition, deterrent and retributive aims recognized in this Court’s cases, and enforcement backed by criminal-process tools—are sufficiently punitive to trigger Ex Post Facto protection when applied to pre-enactment conduct. That conclusion follows from what our precedents actually hold about federal restitution’s role in sentencing, and it avoids the doctrinal and administrability problems that would arise from treating a core sentencing component as “civil” for constitutional purposes. Because applying the MVRA retroactively can increase a defendant’s financial exposure and enforcement consequences compared to the law at the time of the offense, the Ex Post Facto Clause is implicated.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: The MVRA’s text and structure place restitution inside the criminal sentencing scheme: it is imposed only upon conviction, is mandatory, and is administered through § 3664’s sentencing procedures rather than a freestanding civil cause of action—choices we must give effect to rather than recast as mere compensation. That placement is confirmed by the mechanism’s function as a forward-looking penal tool (deterrence and rehabilitation) enforced through uniquely criminal collection consequences, making it more than an administrative device to restore victims. Under the Smith/Hudson framework, those features supply strong indicia of punitive effect, so applying later-enacted MVRA rules to pre-enactment conduct triggers the Ex Post Facto Clause’s prohibition on retroactively increasing criminal punishment. Treating restitution as nonpunitive here would let the “civil label” swallow the constitutional rule whenever Congress routes a sanction through sentencing.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: The operative statutory scheme makes restitution under the MVRA part of the criminal sentence: it is triggered only “when sentencing a defendant convicted” of specified crimes, is imposed through sentencing procedures, and is enforced through mechanisms that attach to the criminal judgment, not a freestanding civil cause of action. Legislating against the settled constitutional backdrop that the Ex Post Facto Clause bars retroactive increases in “punishment,” Congress’s choice to make restitution mandatory and sentence-integrated reflects a penal measure, not merely victim compensation. That understanding is confirmed by statutory context and this Court’s descriptions of federal restitution as serving punitive ends—deterrence, retribution, and rehabilitation—alongside remediation, which is enough to treat it as punishment for ex post facto purposes when later-enacted MVRA rules increase a defendant’s exposure compared to the law at the time of the offense. Accordingly, retroactive application of the MVRA’s restitution regime triggers ex post facto scrutiny because it operates as criminal punishment imposed at sentencing for past conduct.
